original_value: Continuous joint angle estimation based on a surface electromyography (sEMG) signal can be used to improve the man-machine coordination performance of the exoskeleton. In this study, we proposed a time-advanced feature and utilized long short-term memory (LSTM) with a root mean square (RMS) feature and its time-advanced feature (RMSTAF; collectively referred to as RRTAF) of sEMG to estimate the knee joint angle. To evaluate the effect of joint angle estimation, we used root mean square error (RMSE) and cross-correlation coefficient ρ between the estimated angle and actual angle. We also compared three methods (i.e., LSTM using RMS, BPNN (back propagation neural network) using RRTAF, and BPNN using RMS) with LSTM using RRTAF to highlight its good performance. Five healthy subjects participated in the experiment and their eight muscle (i.e., rectus femoris (RF), biceps femoris (BF), semitendinosus (ST), gracilis (GC), semimembranosus (SM), sartorius (SR), medial gastrocnemius (MG), and tibialis anterior (TA)) sEMG signals were taken as algorithm inputs. Moreover, the knee joint angles were used as target values. The experimental results showed that, compared with LSTM using RMS, BPNN using RRTAF, and BPNN using RMS, the average RMSE values of LSTM using RRTAF were respectively reduced by 8.57%, 46.62%, and 68.69%, whereas the average ρ values were respectively increased by 0.31%, 4.15%, and 18.35%. The results demonstrated that LSTM using RRTAF, which contained the time-advanced feature, had better performance for estimating the knee joint motion.

result.paraphrase: Continuous knee joint angle estimation from a surface electromyography (sEMG) signal can improve man-machine coordination in exoskeletons. In this study, we introduced a time-advanced feature and used long short-term memory (LSTM) with the root mean square (RMS) feature and its time-advanced counterpart (RMSTAF; collectively called RRTAF) of sEMG to estimate knee angle. Estimation performance was assessed with root mean square error (RMSE) and the cross-correlation coefficient ρ between the estimated and actual angles. We further compared LSTM using RRTAF with three methods—LSTM using RMS, BPNN (back propagation neural network) using RRTAF, and BPNN using RMS—to demonstrate its superior performance. Five healthy subjects took part in the experiment, and sEMG signals from eight muscles—rectus femoris (RF), biceps femoris (BF), semitendinosus (ST), gracilis (GC), semimembranosus (SM), sartorius (SR), medial gastrocnemius (MG), and tibialis anterior (TA)—were used as algorithm inputs. The knee joint angles served as target values. Experimental results showed that, relative to LSTM using RMS, BPNN using RRTAF, and BPNN using RMS, the average RMSE of LSTM using RRTAF decreased by 8.57%, 46.62%, and 68.69%, respectively, while the average ρ increased by 0.31%, 4.15%, and 18.35%, respectively. These findings indicate that LSTM using RRTAF, which includes the time-advanced feature, performs better for estimating knee joint motion.
